## Bands, pirates and outlaws

**Bands are a character's soldiers (decided 21 October 2026).** A character has no land to levy from, so his soldiers are a band: men he gathers from a province's loose people and pays in gold or the promise of loot, as many as the province has and as he can pay and feed. A band fights by the same rules as any unit. Unpaid or unfed, it melts back into the loose men or turns on its leader, as servants leave a master who does not pay. When a king or a character hires a band, the contract is with its leader, a character, and the men follow him: if he is bribed or turns, the band goes with him. A power may also lend or give troops to a character, as it can to another power, and they become his band under the same rule. This covers the mercenary captain who hires his company out to kings and the Habiru chief who robs caravans alike ("Going outlaw", "Pirates and bandits").

**How many bands (decided 27 October 2026).** No number sets how many bands a land holds or how large they grow. Men join whichever band gives each the best share, as they choose between the land and the road ("Bandits rob the purse"), and a leader keeps only as many as he can pay and feed. So a large lawless land usually holds several small bands competing for men and roads: a chief who wins draws men from those who lose, and one grown past what he can feed frays or splits ("A band that loses its leader" under "A head rises where men lack one"). Chiefs are characters like any other, with no rules of their own: they treat, swear pacts and betray, fight over a road whose haul two bands would split, sell each other to a king for a price, and hire on with kings or with each other, their men following them ("Anyone can hire anyone"). One chief gathering the others under him is the rare and dangerous case, as Abdi-Ashirta gathered the Habiru of Amurru, and kings have the means to stop it: buy off a lieutenant, pay one chief to turn on another, or march in before he grows. Script chiefs play it well, raiding where it pays, joining the stronger and bargaining with kings, or the tuning would measure bad play. How large a crowd raises a chief, and how often, are first guesses in item 11b; item 18 tunes them against the sources: most bands from tens of men to a few hundred, a chief uniting others a few times in a game, and a king who lets policing lapse paying for it plainly, while one who polices gains by it.

**A head rises where men lack one (decided 21 October 2026).** Where men act together without a leader, one of their own may step forward and become a character, speaking what they speak. One rule covers every case, each built with its own system:

- **A crowd of loose men.** Loose men drift and rob without a leader ("Bandits rob the purse"), but a crowd large enough, in any land policed too little, held or not (at the start, where the vassal letters show the Habiru, as "Starting positions come from the sources" says), raises a chief who gathers it into a band ("Bands are a character's soldiers" above). Each season a crowd has a chance to raise a chief, greater the larger it is and smaller where a band already works nearby, whose men it would join instead; the seed draws it, so a replay raises the same chiefs (decided 27 October 2026). Item 11b.
- **A band that loses its leader,** killed, captured or turned on: one of its own takes over, or it melts back into the loose men. A band grown too large for its leader to pay and feed, or too poor to keep, may split instead of melting away: an able one of its own walks off with the men who follow him, as a band of his own (decided 27 October 2026). Pirates are bands at sea and follow the same rule. Item 11b.
- **Mutineers.** A unit that mutinies for hunger or missing pay disbands until item 11b; from then on it may follow one of its own as a band instead ("Armies need food as well as pay"). Item 11b.
- **A fallen kingdom's army with no commander** may raise a captain from its ranks instead of disbanding, and he faces the commander's choice ("A kingdom falls with its capital"). Item 13, with commanders.
- **A revolt with no leader.** Land that breaks free with no governor or commander at its head ("How cities become free") is lawless until a ruler rises from its own people at the pace its people set ("A head rises in time"), and he then rules it as a power with a seat of its own, as every city-state is from item 11+ ("Minds follow what is at stake"). Item 17.
- **A fallen court's people.** When a kingdom falls, its court's characters have lost their employer and seek work like anyone, and its refugees are loose men, from whom a head may rise as from any crowd (decided 27 October 2026), carrying the court's language and some of what it knew; whatever he claims for himself is words, since the game has no heirs. Item 11b.

**Land without a ruler (decided 27 October 2026).** A province that no power holds and no ruler governs is not a kind of state with rules of its own: it is what the general rules make of land nobody governs, and any province can come to it. None starts so (decided 27 October 2026): in 1346 every land had a head, if only a chief, so the Kaska lands, Lukka and the Sutean steppe each start under one leader of its own, as a city-state does ("Starting positions come from the sources"). The Habiru are no land: they are loose men, wherever men were uprooted ("Across borders, people flee"). In play a province comes to it when its holder loses it and nobody takes it up: a kingdom fallen with its capital whose land nobody occupies ("A kingdom falls with its capital"), a governor gone with no one to follow him, a revolt that breaks a province free before anyone leads it.

- **Nobody to deal with.** There is no seat, no treasury and nobody to seal a tablet, so the land itself can be bought, promised or agreed to by nobody until someone rules it. A chief who rises there is a character with his band, speaking for himself and never for the land; he rules it only once he has taken and held it ("A head rises in time"). Its people pay no tax and keep what they produce, and its market is open to whoever comes.
- **What was built stays, unpaid.** Its walls, roads and harbours remain and decay without upkeep, like anyone's unpaid buildings ("One rule for everything built"). A land that starts without a ruler starts with what the sources give it, which is usually little.
- **Nobody polices it,** so its loose men rob the roads and, on a coast, the sea, and the road's check is harsher there ("Bandits rob the purse", "Interception on the road").
- **Anyone may march in,** with nobody to stop them but its people. Holding it is conquest like any other, absorbed slowly and, from item 17, as restless as its conditions make it ("Slow absorption", "Revolt follows conditions, not dice").
- **A head rises in time,** at a pace set by its people, not by a type: a walled town with an elite of its own soon raises a ruler from among them ("A revolt with no leader"), a thin land of herders and loose men gathers only bands behind chiefs ("A crowd of loose men"), and a chief who holds a land long enough comes to rule it, with a seat of his own: the new Idrimi (item 17).

Each part is built with its own system: loose men in item 10+, bands and chiefs in 11b, policing and upkeep in 15, rulers rising in 17. Nothing is built for the type, since there is none.

Four rules hold throughout. Not every body finds a head: the chance grows with its size and with how long it has gone without one, so a small mutiny melts away and a large one finds its man. Need comes before the baseline: a body without a head has its chance whatever the pool's size, and the man who rises counts in the pool like anyone else, so strangers come more rarely while it is full ("A baseline, not a limit"). How he rose shapes who he is: his traits are seeded like anyone's but leaned by the circumstance, since the circumstance picks the man, so whoever takes over a mutinous army is bold and ambitious, and the scribe who leads a fallen court's refugees is careful. And a body with a paymaster never raises its own head: an army paid and fed has its king, so a head rises only where that bond is broken, and commanders keep their worth. Everything is drawn from the seeded stream ("Deterministic").

**Pirates are bands at sea (decided 21 October 2026).** A pirate crew is a band with a ship, and needs nothing else of its own:

- **The men** are loose men of coastal provinces: fishermen in a bad year, and sailors of a fleet disbanded in a foreign port, by the same rule as an army disbanded abroad.
- **The ship** is bought in a port, taken, or given by a power, as troops can be. A power that gives a band a ship has sponsored piracy it can deny ("Deniable attacks").
- **The waters** are sea zones off coasts with little policing, where pirates intercept shipments and envoys at sea, as the Lukka raided Alashiya. A ship is a unit like a power's fleet and fights by the same rules.

Unpaid or unfed, a crew melts away or turns on its captain like any band.

**Turning outlaw.** A character takes to the hills or the sea when its life pushes it there and its temperament allows:

- **No work and no prospects:** long without employment, especially with a public blemish (a known defector, an exposed liar) or courts that will not hire him.
- **Poverty:** a purse run down by living costs, an unpaid fee, a lost employer.
- **Temperament:** high courage or boldness, low loyalty, high greed or ambition. A timid, loyal man starves quietly; a bold, greedy one takes to the road.
- **Opportunity:** being in or near a lawless province or pirate waters with a band to join. War, disaster or a fallen kingdom nearby makes it likelier.
- **Fear:** rumours of a cruel court can make the hills look safer.

Turning outlaw is no option of its own (decided 27 October 2026): a character turns outlaw by what he does, gathering a band from a province's loose men, joining one or robbing travellers ("Bands are a character's soldiers"). A script character weighs these pressures by formula when it chooses among its ordinary actions, and a model character sees them in its situation and decides; its reason is logged either way ("a year without work, an empty purse, and Amurru was lawless"). It then lives the outlaw's life: which roads or waters to work, whether to rob caravans or sell the band as mercenaries, how to answer a king's pardon or bribe, what to claim when accused.

**The way back** follows the same rule. A king may offer a chief a pardon and paid work by envoy or tablet like any other offer, and a chief who takes it carries the hidden fact "rode with the Habiru". An ambitious chief with a large band may instead reach for a city: the Idrimi path, which leads into the promotion of minor actors.
